title: Singular Value Decomposition
body:
**Every** matrix factors as

$$
A = U\Sigma V^T
$$

with $A$ of size $m \times n$, $U$ ($m \times m$) and $V$ ($n \times n$)
[[Orthonormal Basis|orthogonal]], and $\Sigma$ ($m \times n$) diagonal with non-negative entries
$\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0$ down the diagonal. Those are the **singular values**,
the columns of $U$ are the **left singular vectors** and the columns of $V$ the **right** ones.

The word doing the work is *every*. [[Diagonalization]] needs a square matrix with enough
independent eigenvectors and can simply fail; the [[Spectral Theorem]] needs symmetry. The SVD
needs nothing. Rectangular, singular, defective, all fine. **It is the factorisation that always
exists**, which is why it is the one numerical software reaches for.

## Where it comes from

$A^TA$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite (see [[Quadratic Form]]), so the
[[Spectral Theorem]] applies to it:

- $V$ = the orthonormal eigenvectors of $A^TA$
- $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$, the square roots of its eigenvalues, hence real and $\geq 0$
- $U$ = the orthonormal eigenvectors of $AA^T$, equivalently $\mathbf{u}_i = A\mathbf{v}_i/\sigma_i$

So the SVD is the [[Spectral Theorem]] applied twice, once on each side, to the two symmetric
matrices a rectangular $A$ can make. The defining relation is worth remembering as the pair

$$
A\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i, \qquad A^T\mathbf{u}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{v}_i
$$

which is $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ with the input and output directions allowed to differ.
That is the exact point where eigenvectors fail for non-square matrices: "same direction out as
in" is not a question you can ask when the input and output live in different spaces, so the SVD
asks for two directions instead of one.

## The geometry

Read $A\mathbf{x} = U\Sigma V^T\mathbf{x}$ right to left:

1. $V^T$ **rotates** (or reflects): it re-expresses $\mathbf{x}$ in the $\mathbf{v}_i$ basis.
2. $\Sigma$ **stretches** each axis by $\sigma_i$, and pads or truncates dimensions.
3. $U$ **rotates** into the output space.

**Every linear map is a rotation, a stretch, and another rotation.** Nothing else. The image of
the unit sphere under $A$ is an ellipsoid whose semi-axes are the $\sigma_i$ pointing along the
$\mathbf{u}_i$, so $\sigma_1$ is the largest stretch $A$ can apply to any unit vector (the
spectral norm in [[Vector Norm]]) and $\sigma_n$ the smallest.

## The sum-of-rank-ones form

Multiplying out gives the version everything downstream uses:

$$
A = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i\, \mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{v}_i^T
$$

where $r = \text{rank}(A)$ is the number of non-zero singular values. Each term is a rank-one
matrix, and they are ordered by importance. **Truncate the sum and you have the best possible
approximation of that rank**, which is [[Low-Rank Approximation]] and the reason the SVD is a
compression algorithm as much as a factorisation.

The four fundamental subspaces fall out as a bonus, orthonormal bases included:

| Subspace | Basis |
|---|---|
| column space (range) | $\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_r$ |
| left null space | $\mathbf{u}_{r+1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_m$ |
| row space | $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_r$ |
| null space ([[Kernel and Range|kernel]]) | $\mathbf{v}_{r+1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_n$ |

Rank-nullity is visible in the shape of $\Sigma$. Numerically this is how rank is *actually*
determined: count singular values above a tolerance, rather than row-reducing and asking whether
a float is exactly zero.

## Facts

- Singular values are unique; singular **vectors** are not (sign flips, and rotations inside a
  repeated $\sigma$).
- For a symmetric positive definite $A$, $\sigma_i = \lambda_i$ and the SVD is the spectral
  decomposition. In general $\sigma_i = |\lambda_i|$ only for symmetric $A$, and the two have no
  simple relation otherwise.
- $\|A\|_F^2 = \sum\sigma_i^2$ and $\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1$. See [[Vector Norm]].
- The **condition number** is $\sigma_1/\sigma_r$: how much a relative error in $\mathbf{b}$ can
  be amplified in the solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. Large means the answer is not to be
  trusted, and it is invisible to the [[Determinant]].
- $A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^T$ is the [[Pseudoinverse]], so the SVD solves inconsistent and
  underdetermined systems too.
